title: Blood and Tissue Parasites: Malaria and Microfilariae
summary: A bench-level guide to Giemsa thick and thin blood films, the morphology that separates the four classic Plasmodium species (falciparum rings and banana gametocytes, vivax amoeboid trophozoites and Schüffner dots, ovale fimbriated red cells, malariae band forms), qualitative reporting of malaria smears, and the identification of sheathed microfilariae (Wuchereria bancrofti versus Brugia malayi) with Knott's concentration and collection timing, plus the artifacts and exam traps that fake blood parasites.
objectives: Prepare and interpret Giemsa-stained thick films for detection and thin films for species identification of Plasmodium.
Differentiate P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae by red cell changes, trophozoite shape, stippling, and gametocyte morphology.
Report malaria smears qualitatively in line with the local standard operating procedure and explain why a single negative film does not exclude malaria.
Identify Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi microfilariae by sheath and tail nuclei, and select the correct collection time and concentration method.
Recognize EDTA and staining artifacts that mimic blood parasites and apply the classic exam traps to blood film cases.

highYield: Thick films screen for parasitemia (more blood, red cells lysed, parasites concentrated but morphology distorted); thin films identify the Plasmodium species and the stages present.

P. falciparum: delicate rings, several rings per red cell, applique (accolé) forms at the red cell margin, Maurer's clefts, and banana (crescent)-shaped gametocytes - the only gametocyte shape diagnostic at species level.
P. vivax shows amoeboid trophozoites in enlarged, distorted red cells with fine Schüffner dots; P. ovale shows compact trophozoites in oval red cells with fimbriated edges and coarser stippling.
P. malariae shows band-form trophozoites stretched across normal-sized red cells and has quartan (72-hour) fever periodicity.

A single negative blood film does not exclude malaria: repeat thick and thin smears at 12- to 24-hour intervals for two or three additional sets when clinical suspicion is high; report species and stages per local SOP because reporting methods vary.

Microfilariae: W. bancrofti is sheathed with the tail tip free of nuclei and shows nocturnal periodicity (night blood); B. malayi is sheathed with two distinct subterminal tail nuclei; Onchocerca volvulus is demonstrated in skin snips, not blood.

rows: Normal size; multiple infections per cell

quickReview.mnemonic: Four species, four shapes: Falciparum = Fatal crescents (banana gametocytes, multiple delicate rings); Vivax = Very big amoeboid trophozoites in big red cells; Ovale = Oval fimbriated red cells; Malariae = band/Mature belts.

deepStudy.introduction: Blood parasites are still diagnosed the old-fashioned way: a drop of blood, a glass slide, and a Giemsa stain. Malaria remains the highest-stakes call on a blood film, because Plasmodium falciparum can kill within days while the other species relapse or smolder for months, and because the species name dictates the drugs used. The filarial nematodes are slower but equally morphology-dependent - Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi cause lymphatic filariasis, and the laboratory must know when to draw the blood (at night) and how to concentrate it when microfilariae are scarce. This lesson walks through the thick-film and thin-film workflow, the morphology of the four classic Plasmodium species, how malaria results are reported and qualified, and the sheathed microfilariae that appear on the same stains. Throughout, the practical theme is that artifacts on stored EDTA blood imitate parasites, and that knowing what a smear cannot say is as important as recognizing what it shows.

sections.heading: Thick and thin films: the technique that decides the diagnosis
sections.body: Every malaria workup begins with two smears from the same specimen. The thick film spreads a larger drop of blood several cells deep; during Giemsa staining the red cells are lysed, so the film becomes a concentrated field of leukocytes and any parasites within them. That volume advantage makes the thick film the screening test of choice for low-level parasitemia, but lysis destroys red cell context and distorts parasite shape, so the thick film answers only one question: are parasites present? The thin film is a true monolayer made the same way as a differential smear. Because the red cells stay intact, the technologist can judge red cell size and shape, stippling, and parasite morphology - this is where species identification and staging happen. Both films are air-dried; the thin film is methanol-fixed (the thick film is not), and both are stained in buffered water at the pH recommended by the stain manufacturer, commonly around pH 7.2. Dirty buffer and mistimed staining are the usual culprits when morphology disappoints. Smears should be prepared promptly after collection: delay in a lavender-top EDTA tube allows degenerative changes in both cells and parasites. Examination follows a fixed order - scan the thick film first at low power to establish presence or absence, then move to the thin film monolayer to name the species and list the stages seen: rings, trophozoites, schizonts, and gametocytes.

sections.heading: Plasmodium morphology: the four-species lineup
sections.body: Plasmodium falciparum earns its reputation from three film findings. Rings are delicate, often double or triple within one red cell, and may sit at the cell margin in applique (accolé) form, with the cytoplasm pressed against the membrane as if stuck on. Bluish Maurer's clefts may stipple the infected cell. As infection matures, the diagnostic gametocyte appears: banana- or crescent-shaped, the only gametocyte morphology that names a species at a glance. Falciparum schizonts sequester in deep vessels and are rarely seen in peripheral blood - their absence is expected, not reassuring. Plasmodium vivax prefers young red cells, which enlarge and distort; its trophozoites are amoeboid, spreading irregularly like melting wax, and fine pink Schüffner dots fill the cytoplasm. Plasmodium ovale also shows Schüffner-type stippling (often described as coarser James dots), but the infected red cell stays oval with fimbriated, tufted edges and the trophozoite remains compact and rounded - it does not wander like vivax. Plasmodium malariae infects normal-sized red cells and classically forms band trophozoites stretched across the cell like a belt; its schizonts cluster merozoites into a rosette, and the clinical cycle is quartan (72 hours). RBC preference is a quiet giveaway: vivax and ovale favor younger cells and may be scarce in heavy parasitemia, while falciparum infects cells of all ages and can reach very high counts.

sections.heading: Reporting the smear and the artifact trap
sections.body: Malaria smears are reported in words first: species identified, and the stages present. Many laboratories add a measure of parasite density - percent parasitemia on the thin film, or parasites per unit volume against a leukocyte count - but methods vary between laboratories, so the report must state the method used and follow the local standard operating procedure rather than any universal cutoff. A negative report is worded with equal care. 'No parasites seen' describes that specimen at that moment; it does not exclude malaria, because parasitemia fluctuates as broods mature and sequester. When suspicion persists, the standard practice is to repeat thick and thin films at 12- to 24-hour intervals for two or three additional sets before malaria is considered excluded. Rapid antigen tests (HRP2 and pLDH assays) support the diagnosis but do not replace microscopy for species and staging, and HRP2 deletions in some P. falciparum populations can make antigen tests falsely negative. The counterweight to overcalling is artifact. A platelet lying on top of a red cell mimics a ring form with pseudo-chromatin; stain precipitate deposits blue granules that fake stippling or intracellular parasites; Howell-Jolly bodies appear as single round inclusions in asplenic patients. Smears made hours after collection from EDTA blood exaggerate all of these. The discipline is simple: confirm that the suspect structure lies within the red cell cytoplasm, is consistent in size and staining with a real stage, and appears in a believable pattern across the monolayer before calling it.

sections.heading: Microfilariae: sheaths, tails, and timing
sections.body: Lymphatic filariasis is caused by sheathed microfilariae that circulate in blood, and the two exam-relevant species are told apart by the tail. Wuchereria bancrofti, the global heavyweight, has a sheath that stains faintly and a column of body nuclei that stops short of the pointed tail tip, leaving the tip itself clear. Its microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity: they appear in peripheral blood at night, so specimens are drawn roughly between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. (some Pacific strains are subperiodic, and local epidemiology adjusts the timing). Brugia malayi is also sheathed, but its tail carries two distinct subterminal nuclei just below the tip - the signature contrast with Wuchereria. Clinical context differs too: bancroftian filariasis brings hydrocele and lymphedema of the legs and genitals, while brugian disease favors limb lymphedema in rural Southeast Asia. Two relatives complete the picture. Loa loa travels in daytime blood, has a sheath that stains poorly and nuclei that run all the way to the tail tip, and announces itself with transient Calabar subcutaneous swellings and marked eosinophilia. Onchocerca volvulus is not a blood microfilaria at all - its unsheathed larvae live in skin, recovered by skin snips, and cause river blindness. When microfilariae are scanty, concentration methods win: in Knott's concentration, blood is mixed with a lysing fixative such as 2 percent formalin, centrifuged, and the sediment is stained and examined; membrane filtration is an alternative. A thick film alone can miss low-density carriers, and density counts matter for treatment decisions and for safety when microfilaremic patients receive certain drugs.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Identifying P. falciparum is an emergency-level result: sequestration, severe anemia, cerebral malaria, and death can follow quickly, and the finding must reach the clinician without delay. Species identification also drives cure strategy - P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites that relapse from the liver, so radical cure requires a 8-aminoquinoline (primaquine or tafenoquine) with G6PD testing first, while falciparum and malariae have no hypnozoite stage. Misreading ovale as vivax (or the reverse) is usually survivable; missing falciparum is not. For the filarial worms, chronic infection produces lymphedema and elephantiasis, hydrocele, and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (nocturnal cough and wheeze with towering eosinophils and IgE, usually occult W. bancrofti). Mass drug administration programs use diethylcarbamazine with albendazole or ivermectin with albendazole, and ivermectin treats onchocerciasis - but it must be used with great caution where Loa loa microfilaremia is heavy, because rapid killing of Loa microfilariae can precipitate severe encephalopathic reactions. For the bench, the message is that a name on a smear changes treatment within hours, and eosinophilia on a concurrent CBC is a standing invitation to look for worms.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Read malaria films against the whole picture: travel or residence history, fever pattern, platelet count (thrombocytopenia is common in acute malaria), and anemia. Eosinophilia points toward tissue-invasive helminths and filariasis rather than uncomplicated malaria. Correlate thick and thin films - presence on thick film with species on thin film - and state in the report whether quantitation was done and by which method, since reporting methods vary. A negative film in a febrile traveler is a prompt for serial re-examination at 12- to 24-hour intervals, not a closed case, and the report should say when and how the specimen was collected. Interpret suspicious structures skeptpectively: verify that putative parasites are inside red cells on the thin film, not floating between cells or perched on top of them; delayed EDTA specimens distort trophozoite shape and fade stippling, and stain precipitate mimics everything. For microfilariae, note the collection time in the report (night versus day) and the method (thick film versus Knott's concentration), because a negative daytime film for suspected bancroftian filariasis may simply mean the blood was drawn at the wrong hour.

examTraps: P. vivax versus P. ovale: both show Schüffner-type dots, but ovale red cells are oval with fimbriated edges and the trophozoite is compact, while vivax red cells are enlarged and distorted with amoeboid trophozoites. Ovale schizonts carry up to 8 merozoites versus 12-24 in vivax.

EDTA artifacts: a platelet overlying a red cell fakes a ring form with pseudo-chromatin, and stain precipitate fakes stippling or intracellular parasites. Smears should be prepared promptly, and a real parasite lies inside the red cell cytoplasm with consistent size and staining across the monolayer.

Only P. falciparum gametocytes are banana-shaped; round gametocytes in an enlarged stippled red cell favor P. vivax or P. ovale. Do not speciate from a gametocyte alone - use the red cell changes and the rings.

A single negative smear never excludes malaria. Repeat thick and thin films at 12- to 24-hour intervals for two or three additional sets, and remember that qualitative versus parasitemia reporting methods vary by laboratory - follow the local SOP.

Microfilariae: W. bancrofti tail tips are free of nuclei; B. malayi tails carry two subterminal nuclei. Both need night blood; Loa loa needs day blood; Onchocerca is in skin snips, never in peripheral blood.

Falciparum schizonts are absent from peripheral blood because they sequester - their absence on a smear does not argue against falciparum, and high parasitemia with only rings is classic severe-risk falciparum.

memoryHooks.text: Banana gametocytes = falciparum; band forms = malariae; big amoeboid trophozoites = vivax; oval fimbriated red cells = ovale.
memoryHooks.funny: Meow the cat: 'Pag may banana sa dugo, hindi yan turon - P. falciparum yan! Band form naman ang P. malariae, parang belt na naka-stretch sa gitna ng RBC. Kawawang RBC, na-stretch na sa exam, na-stretch pa sa binti pag namiss mo ang diagnosis!'

memoryHooks.text: Night blood (around 10 p.m. to 2 a.m.) for W. bancrofti and B. malayi; tail-tip nuclei separate Brugia (two subterminal nuclei) from Wuchereria (clear tip).
memoryHooks.funny: 'Wag kang kukuha ng dugo para sa microfilariae ng tanghali - tulog pa ang mga yan! Night shift ang W. bancrofti at B. malayi, day shift naman si Loa loa, parang mga kaklase mong gising lang kapag exam na. Si Onchocerca? Hindi yan sa dugo - nasa balat, tamad lumabas!'
